title: Adding and removing array items - push, unset, array_push, array_pop
answer: Append with [] or array_push. Remove the last item with array_pop and the first with array_shift. unset removes one item but leaves a gap in the numbering, so re-index with array_values when order matters.
pitfall: After unset, count and indexes no longer line up. If you loop expecting 0, 1, 2 in order, call array_values first.

title: Counting and checking arrays - count, empty, is_array, array_key_exists
answer: count returns how many items an array has. empty is true for an empty array, and also for null, false, 0 and an empty string, so it does not prove a value is an array. is_array proves the type, and array_key_exists proves a key exists even when its value is null.
pitfall: isset returns false for a key whose value is null, even though the key exists. Use array_key_exists when null is a valid value.

title: Destructuring and spread - list(), short syntax, and ... unpacking
answer: List assignment pulls array values into separate variables in one line. The spread operator unpacks arrays into a new array or into function arguments. Spread with string keys overwrites earlier values with later ones.
pitfall: Unpacking a string-keyed array into another array with ... keeps later values only for duplicate keys, which can silently drop data.

title: array_map, array_filter, array_reduce - transform arrays without loops
answer: array_map applies a function to every item and returns a new array. array_filter keeps only items that pass a test. array_reduce combines all items into one value, such as a total. They do not change the original array.
pitfall: array_filter keeps the original keys, so a filtered list can have gaps. Call array_values on the result before encoding it as JSON, or it becomes an object.

title: Merging and searching arrays - merge, in_array, array_search, array_column
keywords: array me value hai ya nahi
answer: array_merge combines arrays. in_array checks whether a value exists, and array_search returns its key or false. array_column pulls one field out of a list of records. Pass true as the third argument to in_array and array_search for strict type comparison.
pitfall: Without strict mode, in_array('2', [2]) is true because PHP converts types. For IDs and tokens, always pass true.

title: Sorting arrays - sort, rsort, asort, ksort, usort
answer: sort re-indexes and sorts values. asort keeps keys attached to values. ksort sorts by key. usort sorts with your own comparison function, for example by a field inside each item. Sorting functions change the array in place and return true or false, not the sorted array.
pitfall: sort returns a boolean, not the array. Writing $sorted = sort($arr) gives you true, not a sorted array.

title: Arrays - indexed, associative, and nested arrays
answer: An indexed array uses numbers starting at 0. An associative array uses named keys. Arrays can hold other arrays. Access values with square brackets, and check a key exists with isset before reading it.
pitfall: Reading a key that does not exist raises a warning. Use ?? or isset first, especially with user-supplied data.

title: Looping arrays - foreach with keys, values, and references
keywords: array ke har item par kaam
answer: foreach reads every item without managing an index. Use key => value when you need the key too. A & reference lets you change items in place, but you must unset the reference variable afterwards or it keeps pointing at the last item.
pitfall: Forgetting unset($n) after a reference loop leaves $n bound to the last element, and later assignments to $n silently change your array.
